analysis.one_liner: Restores the estate tax to 2009 rates and sends the revenue to Social Security.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in March 2026 and referred to the Finance Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bring the estate tax back to its 2009 form: a top rate of 45% on estates above $1.5 million, a $3.5 million exemption per person instead of the much larger current exemption, and a tighter $1 million cap on tax-free lifetime gifts. It would also route all estate and gift tax revenue directly into a combined Social Security Trust Fund. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2026 and has not moved since, with no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries would gain a new revenue stream aimed at shoring up the trust fund that pays their benefits. Middle-class heirs of estates between $1 million and $3.5 million could also see a modest tax break relative to current law, since the 2009 rate schedule applies lower rates to smaller estates even as the exemption drops.

how_it_helps.text: The bill returns the estate tax rate to 2009 levels, taxing estates above $1.5 million at a top rate of 45%, and lowers the amount exempted from estate tax to $3.5 million per person.
It lowers the lifetime gift-tax exemption to $1 million, limiting how much wealth can be passed to heirs tax-free during life, and caps how much unused exemption a surviving spouse can inherit.
It directs 100% of estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax revenue into the Social Security Trust Fund, providing new funding for retirement and disability benefits.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy families with estates over $3.5 million, who would pay up to 45% tax on the amount above that threshold, and wealthy individuals making lifetime gifts above $1 million. Very few ordinary households would owe any new tax under this bill.

drawbacks.text: The 45% rate above $1.5 million and the $3.5 million exemption would raise taxes on some family businesses and farms at inheritance time, and critics argue this can force heirs to sell assets to pay the tax.

With no cosponsors and only a referral to committee, the bill is unlikely to advance in this Congress, so its promised Social Security strengthening would not materialize even if the underlying idea is sound.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — restoring a 45% estate tax above $1 million and directing the revenue to Social Security — is real but arrives only if the bill becomes law, and it faces long odds in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 seats and tax increases on inherited wealth have not advanced in years. The costs are modest and fall on a small number of large estates and wealthy families. The main drawback is political rather than substantive: a bill with no cosponsors has almost no path forward, so its stated benefit is likely to remain theoretical.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee after introduction and has not moved since, with no other senators signing on.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 25, 2026 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action has been taken on the bill since its referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy families planning large inheritances benefit from the bill's stagnation, since their estates continue to face the lower current exemption and rates rather than the 2009-level tax this bill proposed.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Hold 55 seats and have generally opposed raising the estate tax; no committee action has been scheduled.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no meaningful pattern of support or opposition has formed.

industries.note: Their heirs would pay up to 45% tax on the portion of an estate above $3.5 million, and lifetime gifts above $1 million would be taxed, reversing years of steadily higher exemptions.

industries.industry: Estate planning and tax advisory services
industries.note: A larger portion of wealthy families' assets would be exposed to the estate tax, reducing demand for complex avoidance structures, though planning work would continue.

industries.industry: Lobbying and advocacy groups for estate tax repeal
industries.note: Groups that have pushed to keep the estate tax low would face renewed pressure to defend current exemption levels.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action more than a month after introduction, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress. Estate tax increases are a low priority for the Senate majority, and the bill would need to clear the Finance Committee and a 60-vote threshold on the floor to move forward. It is most likely to die quietly at the end of the session.
